messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 64
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Politician
- Trauma Type: Relief worker in war zone
- Pcl5: 45

Elias sits across from me, his posture rigid despite the plush office chair. At sixty-four, his face bears the same weathered lines that first appeared decades ago in a displacement camp near the border, where he went not as a statesman, but as a medic with a canvas satchel and a headlamp. He tells me about that year in present tense, as if the dirt and diesel fumes still coat his tongue. He remembers the cadence of distant artillery, the way he learned to read the sky for drop shadows, the weight of a small hand slipping from his grip when a shell fell too close. He speaks of it not with theatrical grief, but with the quiet, methodical precision of a man cataloging evidence. He still performs the same rituals his father taught him in their ancestral courtyard: washing his hands until the skin cracks, arranging his keys in exact alignment, tracing the same worn leather journal that has survived three marriages and two continents. Since returning, life has moved in careful, measured steps. He left the field, built a career, and eventually rose to elected office, where he now negotiates policy and endures the glare of campaign lights. Yet the past does not recognize his current title. When the city’s emergency sirens wail during a summer storm, his breath catches, his shoulders hike to his ears, and his mind instantly maps the nearest exit routes. He avoids driving past the old industrial district, citing construction delays, though we both know the rusted warehouses trigger the memory of the triage tents. He no longer watches news broadcasts featuring foreign conflict, changing channels with a sharp click before the images can take root. His aides report that he leaves strategy meetings when a pen drops or a chair scrapes the floor, claiming he has a prior engagement. He signs bills that allocate millions to overseas aid, yet he cannot sit through a full municipal council meeting without checking his watch, his gaze drifting to the windows as if counting the seconds until an unpredictable breach. The divorce settled quietly two years ago. He says it was a mutual decision, though he admits he stopped believing in shared futures long before the lawyers arrived. He describes himself as a closed ledger, unable to sit with his ex-wife in a room without bracing for the next demand, the next loss. His legislative colleagues note his abrupt departures from evening receptions, his habit of standing near the doors, scanning crowds. He jokes about it lightly, saying the press is worse than the crossfire, but his knuckles whiten around his drink glass. He tells me he stops sleeping past three a.m. He lies awake listening to the hum of the refrigerator, counting the seconds between each mechanical click, convinced it is a countdown. When he does drift off, he wakes drenched, heart hammering, the taste of copper and ash in his mouth. He no longer attends the Friday prayers he once led with the community elders, finding the collective stillness too much to bear. He comes to my office on Thursdays, stepping through the door with the same deliberate caution he uses when approaching a checkpoint. He adjusts his cufflinks, straightens his tie, and sits exactly on the edge of the cushion. He speaks of his current legislative push for refugee resettlement funding, but his voice tightens when he mentions the word camp. He traces the rim of his water glass, watching the condensation pool. He tells me he reads his former colleagues’ names on memorial walls during committee meetings, feeling a familiar hollow pull in his chest. He no longer trusts his own judgment in crowded rooms, second-guessing every gesture, every pause. He tells me he flinches when a waiter drops a tray in the restaurant near the capitol, though no one else seems to notice. He says he is tired of carrying a country that never carried him back. I watch his hands rest on the table, palms flat, fingers occasionally twitching toward nothing. The session ends with him rising slowly, smoothing his jacket, and walking out into the afternoon light as though it were a foreign country.
